Jacob leaves Laban's household (verses 1–21)

Scripture gives us a detailed account of the affairs of these families, while saying nothing about what people would call the great political events of that age.

The Bible is meant to teach ordinary people the duties of daily life: how to serve God, enjoy the blessings he gives, and do good wherever he has placed them.

Selfish people imagine that anything which passes them by has been taken from them.

Greed can become so powerful that it swallows up even natural family affection.

The mistake of placing too high a value on worldly wealth lies at the root of covetousness, envy, and every kind of evil.

People whose hearts are set on this world get in one another's way. Each seems to be taking something from everyone else.

That is how discontent, jealousy, and quarrels grow.

Yet there are other riches, more than enough for everyone. Happy are those who seek them first.

Whenever we move from one place to another, we must pay attention to God's command and trust his promise.

If he is with us, we need not be afraid.

We face so many dangers that nothing else can give our hearts lasting courage.

When difficulties come, remembering earlier times when we enjoyed God's special favor and fellowship is deeply refreshing.

We should also often remember the vows we have made to him, so that we do not fail to keep them.

Laban pursues Jacob, and Rachel's idols are exposed (verses 22–35)

God can put a bridle in the mouths of wicked people and restrain their malice without changing their hearts.

Even when they have no love for God's people, they may pretend otherwise and try to make a virtue of doing what they cannot avoid.

How foolish of Laban to call things his gods when someone could steal them!

Enemies can steal what belongs to us, but they cannot steal our God.

Laban accused Jacob of things Jacob knew nothing about.

Those who entrust their cause to God are still free to defend themselves, provided they do so with gentleness and reverence.

When we read how Rachel stole her father's household images, what a sad picture of wrongdoing appears!

Nahor's family had left the idolatrous Chaldeans. Had that very family now become idolatrous itself?

Yes, it had.

They seem to have been like people in later times who swore both by the Lord and by Malcham (Zephaniah 1:5).

They were also like people in our own day who want to serve both God and wealth.

Many acknowledge the true God with their lips, while their hearts and homes remain full of spiritual idols.

A person who gives himself over to covetousness, as Laban did, has already made the world his god.

He need only live among openly idolatrous people to become an idolater himself—or at least someone who approves of their practices.

Jacob answers Laban (verses 36–42)

Jacob willingly endured the burning heat of day and the freezing cold of night to become Laban's son-in-law.

What, then, should we refuse to endure in order to become children of God?

Jacob spoke of God as his father's God.

He considered himself unworthy of God's attention, yet he was loved for his father's sake.

He called him both the God of Abraham and the Fear of Isaac.

Abraham had died and entered the world where perfect love casts out fear.

Isaac, however, was still alive, honoring the Lord in his heart as the one to be feared and revered.

Jacob and Laban make a covenant at Galeed (verses 43–55)

Laban could neither justify his own conduct nor prove Jacob guilty. So he wanted to hear no more about their dispute.

He would not admit his fault, as he should have done.

Instead, he proposed a covenant of friendship, and Jacob readily agreed.

They raised a heap of stones to preserve the memory of the occasion.

Henry explains this custom by saying that writing was either unknown or little used at that time.

They offered a sacrifice of peace offerings.

Peace with God gives true comfort to the peace we enjoy with our friends.

The two men then ate together, sharing the meal connected with the sacrifice.

In ancient times, people often confirmed covenants of friendship by eating and drinking together.

God is the judge between people who are in dispute, and his judgment is always right.

Whoever does wrong does so at his own peril.

They gave the place a new name meaning “heap of witness.”

After their angry exchange, they parted as friends.

God is often kinder to us than our fears lead us to expect.

He can direct the hearts of others in our favor far beyond anything we anticipated.

Trusting him is never in vain.

[Gen.31.1-Gen.31.21]
Chapter 31
Chapter Outline

Laban pursues Jacob. | (23-35) |
Jacob's complaint of Laban's conduct. | (36-42) |
Their covenant at Galeed. | (43-55) |
Verses 1-21
The affairs of these families are related very minutely, while (what are called) the great events of states and kingdoms at that period, are not mentioned. The Bible teaches people the common duties of life, how to serve God, how to enjoy the blessings he bestows, and to do good in the various stations and duties of life. Selfish men consider themselves robbed of all that goes past them, and covetousness will even swallow up natural affection. Men's overvaluing worldly wealth is that error which is the root of covetousness, envy, and all evil. The men of the world stand in each other's way, and every one seems to be taking away from the rest; hence discontent, envy, and discord. But there are possessions that will suffice for all; happy they who seek them in the first place. In all our removals we should have respect to the command and promise of God. If He be with us, we need not fear. The perils which surround us are so many, that nothing else can really encourage our hearts. To remember favoured seasons of communion with God, is very refreshing when in difficulties; and we should often recollect our vows, that we fail not to fulfil them.
[Gen.31.22-Gen.31.35]
Verses 22-35
God can put a bridle in the mouth of wicked men, to restrain their malice, though he do not change their hearts. Though they have no love to God's people, they will pretend to it, and try to make a merit of necessity. Foolish Laban! to call those things his gods which could be stolen! Enemies may steal our goods, but not our God. Here Laban lays to Jacob's charge things that he knew not. Those who commit their cause to God, are not forbidden to plead it themselves with meekness and fear. When we read of Rachel's stealing her father's images, what a scene of iniquity opens! The family of Nahor, who left the idolatrous Chaldees; is this family itself become idolatrous? It is even so. The truth seems to be, that they were like some in after-times, who sware by the Lord and by Malcham, [Zeph.1.5] Zep 1:5; and like others in our times, who wish to serve both God and mammon. Great numbers will acknowledge the true God in words, but their hearts and houses are the abodes of spiritual idolatry. When a man gives himself up to covetousness, like Laban, the world is his god; and he has only to reside among gross idolaters in order to become one, or at least a favourer of their abominations.
[Gen.31.36-Gen.31.42]
Verses 36-42
If Jacob were willingly consumed with heat in the day, and frost by night, to become the son-in-law of Laban, what should we refuse to endure, to become the sons of God? Jacob speaks of God as the God of his father; he thought himself unworthy to be regarded, but was beloved for his father's sake. He calls him the God of Abraham, and the fear of Isaac; for Abraham was dead, and gone to that world where perfect love casts out fear; but Isaac was yet alive, sanctifying the Lord in his heart, as his fear and his dread.
[Gen.31.43-Gen.31.55]
Verses 43-55
Laban could neither justify himself nor condemn Jacob, therefore desires to hear no more of that matter. He is not willing to own himself in fault, as he ought to have done. But he proposes a covenant of friendship between them, to which Jacob readily agrees. A heap of stones was raised, to keep up the memory of the event, writing being then not known or little used. A sacrifice of peace offerings was offered. Peace with God puts true comfort into our peace with our friends. They did eat bread together, partaking of the feast upon the sacrifice. In ancient times covenants of friendship were ratified by the parties eating and drinking together. God is judge between contending parties, and he will judge righteously; whoever do wrong, it is at their peril. They gave a new name to the place, The heap of witness. After this angry parley, they part friends. God is often better to us than our fears, and overrules the spirits of men in our favour, beyond what we could have expected; for it is not in vain to trust in him.

God's angels meet Jacob, and he fears Esau (verses 1–8)

God's angels appeared to Jacob to encourage him and assure him of divine protection.

When God intends to lead his people through great trials, he often prepares them with great comforts.

Jacob, to whom the promise belonged, had spent years in difficult service, while Esau had become a prince.

Jacob sent a respectful message to his brother, showing that he was not insisting on the rights of the firstborn.

Giving way can calm even serious offenses (Ecclesiastes 10:4).

We should not refuse to speak respectfully even to people who are unjustly angry with us.

Then Jacob heard that Esau was approaching with men prepared for conflict, and he was deeply afraid.

A sharp awareness of danger, and the fear it awakens, can exist alongside humble confidence in God's power and his promises.

Jacob prays and prepares a gift (verses 9–23)

Times of fear should become times of prayer.

Whatever frightens us should drive us to our knees before God.

Jacob had recently seen the angels who guarded him. But in his trouble, he turned to God, not to the angels.

He knew that the angels were servants of God, just as he was (Revelation 22:9).

Jacob's prayer is an excellent model of true prayer.

He gratefully remembered the undeserved kindness God had shown him.

He humbly confessed that he was unworthy of those blessings.

He plainly told God about his fears and his distress.

He placed the entire matter in the Lord's hands and rested all his hopes on him.

The best words we can bring to God in prayer are the words God himself has spoken to us.

In this way, Jacob made the Lord's name his strong tower, where he could find safety.

Fear did not drive Jacob into despair.

Nor did his prayer make him so presumptuous that he neglected the practical means God had given him.

God sometimes answers prayer by showing us how to arrange our affairs wisely.

Jacob sent Esau a gift in the hope of calming his anger.

We must not give up hope of reconciliation, even with those who seem most angry with us.

Jacob wrestles with the Angel (verses 24–32)

Long before daybreak, Jacob was alone, laying his fears more fully before God in prayer.

As he prayed, someone who appeared to be a man wrestled with him.

When the Spirit helps us in our weakness, our deepest and most earnest desires may be more than words can express.

We mean more than we can say. Prayer then truly becomes wrestling with God.

However severely we are tested or discouraged, we may persevere and prevail.

When we prevail with God in prayer, we will also prevail over the enemies who struggle against us.

Wrestling demands strength and unrelenting effort. It is a fitting picture of true faith and prayer.

Jacob held his ground.

The struggle lasted a long time, but it neither shook his faith nor silenced his prayer.

He was determined to receive a blessing. He would rather have every bone put out of joint than leave without one.

Those who seek Christ's blessing must resolve not to give up.

Fervent prayer is effective prayer.

The Angel gave Jacob a lasting mark of honor by changing his name.

Jacob means “supplanter.” From then on, he would be remembered not for clever schemes or cunning, but for genuine courage.

He would be called Israel, “a prince with God”—a greater title than any borne by the powerful rulers of the earth.

A true prince is someone who has power with God.

The people most worthy of honor are those who are strong in prayer.

Having prevailed with God, Jacob would also prevail with people. He would win Esau's favor.

Jacob gave the place a new name: Peniel, meaning “the face of God.”

He called it that because he had seen God's appearance there and received God's favor.

When God honors us, our proper response is to marvel at his grace.

Matthew Henry identifies the Angel who wrestled with Jacob as the second Person of the Holy Trinity.

This is the One who would later be revealed as God in the flesh, dwelling among us in human nature and called Immanuel (Hosea 12:4–5).

Jacob left the encounter limping because of his injured thigh.

That continuing weakness may have kept him from becoming proud of the extraordinary revelations he had received.

The sun rose as Jacob went on his way.

And for every soul that has enjoyed fellowship with God, it is truly a sunrise.

The angels of God appeared to Jacob, to encourage him with the assurance of the Divine protection. When God designs his people for great trials, he prepares them by great comforts. While Jacob, to whom the promise belonged, had been in hard service, Esau was become a prince. Jacob sent a message, showing that he did not insist upon the birth-right. Yielding pacifies great offences, [Eccl.10.4] Ec 10:4. We must not refuse to speak respectfully, even to those unjustly angry with us. Jacob received an account of Esau's warlike preparations against him, and was greatly afraid. A lively sense of danger, and quickening fear arising from it, may be found united with humble confidence in God's power and promise.
[Gen.32.9-Gen.32.23]
Verses 9-23
Times of fear should be times of prayer: whatever causes fear, should drive us to our knees, to our God. Jacob had lately seen his guards of angels, but in this distress he applied to God, not to them; he knew they were his fellow-servants, [Rev.22.9] Re 22:9. There cannot be a better pattern for true prayer than this. Here is a thankful acknowledgement of former undeserved favours; a humble confession of unworthiness; a plain statement of his fears and distress; a full reference of the whole affair to the Lord, and resting all his hopes on him. The best we can say to God in prayer, is what he has said to us. Thus he made the name of the Lord his strong tower, and could not but be safe. Jacob's fear did not make him sink into despair, nor did his prayer make him presume upon God's mercy, without the use of means. God answers prayers by teaching us to order our affairs aright. To pacify Esau, Jacob sent him a present. We must not despair of reconciling ourselves to those most angry against us.
[Gen.32.24-Gen.32.32]
Verses 24-32
A great while before day, Jacob being alone, more fully spread his fears before God in prayer. While thus employed, One in the likeness of a man wrestled with him. When the spirit helpeth our infirmities, and our earnest and vast desires can scarcely find words to utter them, and we still mean more than we can express, then prayer is indeed wrestling with God. However tried or discouraged, we shall prevail; and prevailing with Him in prayer, we shall prevail against all enemies that strive with us. Nothing requires more vigour and unceasing exertion than wrestling. It is an emblem of the true spirit of faith and prayer. Jacob kept his ground; though the struggle continued long, this did not shake his faith, nor silence his prayer. He will have a blessing, and had rather have all his bone put out of joint than go away without one. Those who would have the blessing of Christ, must resolve to take no denial. The fervent prayer is the effectual prayer. The Angel puts a lasting mark of honour upon him, by changing his name. Jacob signifies a supplanter. From henceforth he shall be celebrated, not for craft and artful management, but for true valour. Thou shalt be called Israel, a prince with God, a name greater than those of the great men of the earth. He is a prince indeed that is a prince with God; those are truly honourable that are mighty in prayer. Having power with God, he shall have power with men too; he shall prevail, and gain Esau's favour. Jacob gives a new name to the place. He calls it Peniel, the face of God, because there he had seen the appearance of God, and obtained the favour of God. It becomes those whom God honours, to admire his grace towards them. The Angel who wrestled with Jacob was the second Person in the sacred Trinity, who was afterwards God manifest in the flesh, and who, dwelling in human nature, is called Immanuel, [Hos.12.4] Ho 12:4, [Hos.12.5] 5. Jacob halted on his thigh. It might serve to keep him from being lifted up with the abundance of the revelations. The sun rose on Jacob: it is sun-rise with that soul, which has had communion with God.

Jacob and Esau are reconciled (verses 1–16)

Having committed his situation to God in prayer, Jacob continued on his way.

Whatever happens, nothing can truly harm the person whose heart is firmly fixed on trusting God.

Jacob bowed before Esau.

Humble, submissive behavior can do much to turn away anger.

Esau embraced his brother.

God holds every person's heart in his hands. He can turn it whenever and however he pleases.

It is never useless to trust God or to call upon him in trouble.

When someone's ways please the Lord, God can even make that person's enemies live at peace with him.

Esau received Jacob as his brother, and the two showed one another great tenderness.

Esau asked, “Who are these people with you?”

Jacob answered this ordinary question in a way that revealed his character: he was a man whose eyes were continually turned toward the Lord.

Even after his fear had passed, Jacob urged Esau to accept his gift, and Esau took it.

It is a good thing when faith makes people generous, warmhearted, and openhanded.

But Jacob declined Esau's offer to travel with him.

It is unwise to become too closely attached to powerful relatives who do not fear God.

They may expect us to join in their worldly pleasures, or at least quietly approve of them, even while they criticize or mock our faith.

Such relationships may become a trap for us, or those relatives may take offense at us.

If we truly know the value of our souls, we will risk losing everything rather than placing them in danger.

If we truly love Christ, we will risk losing everything rather than renouncing him.

Finally, notice Jacob's tender concern for his family and his flocks.

It reminds us of the good Shepherd of our souls, who gathers the lambs in his arms, carries them close to his heart, and gently leads those nursing their young (Isaiah 40:11).

As parents, teachers, and pastors, we should all follow his example.

Jacob worships God at his new home (verses 17–20)

Jacob did more than speak words of thanks for the favor God had shown him.

He gave thanks through what he did.

He also maintained faith and worship in his family.

Wherever we have a tent, God should have an altar.

Jacob dedicated his altar to El-Elohe-Israel—“God, the God of Israel.”

In doing so, he honored the one living and true God.

He also honored the God of Israel as the God who had entered into covenant with him.

Israel's God is Israel's glory.

Blessed be his name! He is still the mighty God, the God of Israel.

May we praise his name and rejoice in his love throughout our pilgrimage on earth, and forever in the heavenly Canaan.

Verses 1-16
Jacob, having by prayer committed his case to God, went on his way. Come what will, nothing can come amiss to him whose heart is fixed, trusting in God. Jacob bowed to Esau. A humble, submissive behaviour goes far towards turning away wrath. Esau embraced Jacob. God has the hearts of all men in his hands, and can turn them when and how he pleases. It is not in vain to trust in God, and to call upon him in the day of trouble. And when a man's ways please the Lord he maketh even his enemies to be at peace with him. Esau receives Jacob as a brother, and much tenderness passes between them. Esau asks, Who are those with thee? To this common question, Jacob spoke like himself, like a man whose eyes are ever directed towards the Lord. Jacob urged Esau, though his fear was over, and he took his present. It is well when men's religion makes them generous, free-hearted, and open-handed. But Jacob declined Esau's offer to accompany him. It is not desirable to be too intimate with superior ungodly relations, who will expect us to join in their vanities, or at least to wink at them, though they blame, and perhaps mock at, our religion. Such will either be a snare to us, or offended with us. We shall venture the loss of all things, rather than endanger our souls, if we know their value; rather than renounce Christ, if we truly love him. And let Jacob's care and tender attention to his family and flocks remind us of the good Shepherd of our souls, who gathers the lambs with his arm, and carries them in his bosom, and gently leads those that are with young, [Isa.40.11] Is 40:11. As parents, teachers or pastors, we should all follow his example.
[Gen.33.17-Gen.33.20]
Verses 17-20
Jacob did not content himself with words of thanks for God's favour to him, but gave real thanks. Also he kept up religion, and the worship of God in his family. Where we have a tent, God must have an altar. Jacob dedicated this altar to the honour of El-elohe-Israel, God, the God of Israel; to the honour of God, the only living and true God; and to the honour of the God of Israel, as a God in covenant with him. Israel's God is Israel's glory. Blessed be his name, he is still the mighty God, the God of Israel. May we praise his name, and rejoice in his love, through our pilgrimage here on earth, and for ever in the heavenly Canaan.

Dinah and Shechem (verses 1–19)

Young people, especially young women, are safest and best cared for under the protection of godly parents.

Their lack of experience exposes them to danger, as do the flattery and schemes of wicked people who deliberately set traps for them.

They place themselves at risk when they are eager to go out, especially alone, among people who do not share true faith.

Parents are seriously at fault when they fail to prevent their children from exposing themselves to needless danger.

Children who have been allowed to do whatever they please, as Henry describes Dinah, often bring grief and shame to their families.

Dinah's stated purpose was to visit the daughters of the land—to see how they dressed and danced, and what was fashionable among them.

But Henry argues that she wanted not only to see others, but also to be seen herself.

She sought the acquaintance of the Canaanites and wanted to learn their ways.

Consider what followed from Dinah's restless wandering.

The beginning of sin is like water breaking through a barrier.

How great a blaze can begin with a small flame!

We should therefore carefully avoid opportunities for sin and even the paths that lead toward it.

Simeon and Levi's revenge against the Shechemites (verses 20–31)

The men of Shechem submitted to a sacred religious rite only because it served their immediate interests.

They wished to please their ruler and enrich themselves.

God was therefore just in bringing punishment upon them.

Nothing offers greater security than genuine religion.

But few things leave people more exposed than a mere pretense of religion.

Yet Simeon and Levi acted with the greatest injustice.

Those who do wicked things under the appearance of serving God are among the worst enemies of the truth.

They harden the hearts of many people, with destructive consequences.

Other people's sins never excuse our own.

How sadly one sin leads to another, spreading devastation like a fire!

Sinful pleasure leads to seduction.

Seduction gives rise to anger; anger develops into a thirst for revenge.

Revenge turns to deceit; deceit ends in murder; and murder is followed by further acts of lawlessness.

Henry concludes that the history of unlawful sexual relationships shows how often such wrongdoing ends in bloodshed—more often, he argues, than other kinds of sin.

Young persons, especially females, are never so safe and well off as under the care of pious parents. Their own ignorance, and the flattery and artifices of designing, wicked people, who are ever laying snares for them, expose them to great danger. They are their own enemies if they desire to go abroad, especially alone, among strangers to true religion. Those parents are very wrong who do not hinder their children from needlessly exposing themselves to danger. Indulged children, like Dinah, often become a grief and shame to their families. Her pretence was, to see the daughters of the land, to see how they dressed, and how they danced, and what was fashionable among them; she went to see, yet that was not all, she went to be seen too. She went to get acquaintance with the Canaanites, and to learn their ways. See what came of Dinah's gadding. The beginning of sin is as the letting forth of water. How great a matter does a little fire kindle! We should carefully avoid all occasions of sin and approaches to it.
[Gen.34.20-Gen.34.31]
Verses 20-31
The Shechemites submitted to the sacred rite, only to serve a turn, to please their prince, and to enrich themselves, and it was just with God to bring punishment upon them. As nothing secures us better than true religion, so nothing exposes us more than religion only pretended to. But Simeon and Levi were most unrighteous. Those who act wickedly, under the pretext of religion, are the worst enemies of the truth, and harden the hearts of many to destruction. The crimes of others form no excuse for us. Alas! how one sin leads on to another, and, like flames of fire, spread desolation in every direction! Foolish pleasures lead to seduction; seduction produces wrath; wrath thirsts for revenge; the thirst of revenge has recourse to treachery; treachery issues in murder; and murder is followed by other lawless actions. Were we to trace the history of unlawful commerce between the sexes, we should find it, more than any other sin, ending in blood.

Jacob returns to Bethel and removes the idols (verses 1–5)

Jacob had forgotten Bethel.

But God reminds those he loves of duties they have neglected. He does this in one way or another, through conscience or through his providence.

When we make a vow to God, we should not delay keeping it.

Yet it is better to fulfill it late than never.

Jacob told his household to prepare not only for the journey, but also for worship.

Those who lead households should use their authority to maintain the worship of God within their families (Joshua 24:15).

The family had to put away its foreign gods.

Even in homes that appear religious and have an altar to God, much may be wrong.

There may be more idols than anyone expects.

The people were told to make themselves clean and change their clothes.

These outward acts were signs of the cleansing and renewal that must take place within the heart.

What good are clean or new clothes if the heart itself is neither clean nor new?

If Jacob had demanded the removal of those idols earlier, his family would have given them up earlier.

Sometimes efforts at reform succeed far better than we thought possible.

Jacob buried the images.

We must separate ourselves completely from our sins, just as we are separated from those who have died and been buried out of sight.

Jacob then moved from Shechem to Bethel.

The Canaanites were deeply angry at Jacob's sons for their brutal treatment of the Shechemites.

But God's power restrained them, and they did not seize the opportunity to take revenge.

The path of duty is the path of safety.

When we are carrying out God's work, we are under his special protection.

God is with us while we are with him. And if he is for us, who can stand against us?

God governs the world through hidden fears in people's minds far more often than we realize.

God renews his covenant with Jacob (verses 6–15)

The comfort believers receive through holy worship does not come chiefly from Bethel, the house of God.

It comes from El-Bethel, the God of that house.

Religious ordinances are empty if we do not meet God through them.

At Bethel, Jacob buried Deborah, Rebekah's nurse.

Her death was deeply mourned.

Long-serving members of a household who have been faithful and helpful deserve respect.

God appeared to Jacob and renewed his covenant with him.

“I am God Almighty”: God is completely sufficient, able to fulfill his promise at the proper time and to support and provide for Jacob in the meantime.

God promised Jacob two things.

He would become the father of a great nation, and he would possess a good land.

Both promises also had a spiritual meaning.

Jacob understood something of that meaning, although not as clearly or fully as we now can.

Christ is the promised Seed, and heaven is the promised land.

The promised Seed is the foundation of all God's favors, and the heavenly inheritance is their crowning completion.

Rachel's death and Benjamin's birth (verses 16–20)

Rachel once cried out passionately, “Give me children, or I will die!”

Now, after bearing children, she died.

The death of the body is the soul's departure into the world of spirits.

When will we learn that God alone truly knows what is best for his people?

In all earthly concerns, the safest course for a Christian is to say sincerely, “It is the Lord; let him do what seems good to him.”

Our safety and comfort lie in submitting our wills to his.

As Rachel was dying, she named her newborn son Ben-Oni, “son of my sorrow.”

Many sons become a source of grief to the mothers who bore them.

Mothers already suffer enough sorrow on account of their children.

Those children should therefore grow up seeking to bring their mothers joy and, as far as possible, make up for some of that grief.

But Jacob did not want every mention of the boy's name to renew the sorrow of Rachel's death.

So he renamed him Benjamin, “son of my right hand.”

The name expressed how dear Benjamin was to him: he would be the support of Jacob's old age, like a staff held in his right hand.

Reuben's sin and Isaac's death (verses 21–29)

The depth of the suffering caused by Reuben's sin is made clear in the brief words, “And Israel heard of it.”

Nothing more is said, but nothing more needs to be said.

Reuben probably thought that his father would never find out.

Yet those who count on keeping their sins secret are usually disappointed.

Scripture records Isaac's age and death, even though he did not die until after Joseph had been sold into Egypt.

Isaac lived for about forty years after he had made arrangements in expectation of his death (Genesis 27:2).

Putting our hearts and households in order early will not make us die even an hour sooner.

But it will help us die much better.

The account specifically mentions that Esau and Jacob were together in harmony at their father's funeral.

This shows how wonderfully God had changed Esau's disposition.

How terrible it is to see relatives quarreling over a little worldly property beside the graves of those they loved!

They do this even though they themselves are not far from the grave.

Esau and his descendants

The family records in this chapter show that God was faithful to his promise to Abraham.

Esau is called Edom here. That name kept alive the memory of his selling his birthright for a single meal.

Esau continued to show the same disregard for sacred and heavenly things.

In outward prosperity and honor, people who belong to God's covenant often fall behind, while those outside the covenant get ahead.

Imagine what a test of faith it must have been for the Israelites, living as slaves in Egypt, to hear about the splendor and power of Edom's kings.

Yet those who expect great things from God must be willing to wait for them.

God's time is always the best time.

Mount Seir is described as the land the Edomites possessed.

Canaan, at that point, was still only the land God had promised to Abraham's descendants.

The Edomites already held Seir, while Israel awaited Canaan.

The children of this world possess all they expect to have now, with nothing left to hope for beyond it (Luke 16:25).

God's children, by contrast, have almost nothing of their full inheritance in hand, but everything to hope for.

When all things are considered, it is incomparably better to have Canaan as a promise than to possess Mount Seir already.

Joseph is loved by Jacob and hated by his brothers (verses 1–4)

Joseph's history points us to Christ, who was humbled before being exalted. It also reflects the Christian's path: we must pass through many troubles before entering the kingdom.

Few accounts show so clearly the good and evil movements of the human heart, or God's remarkable providence in using both to fulfill his purposes.

Although Joseph was his father's favorite, he was not raised to be idle. Parents do not truly love their children when they spare them every task, effort, and hardship.

There is good reason why excessive pampering is called spoiling a child. Those who grow up doing nothing may end up good for nothing.

Yet Jacob made his preference obvious by dressing Joseph more finely than the rest. Parents should not favor one child over another without serious reason arising from their different conduct.

Children soon notice unequal treatment, and quarrels follow. Away from Jacob's supervision, his older sons behaved in ways they would never have dared at home.

Joseph reported their misconduct so that their father could restrain them. He was not spreading gossip to stir up discord; he acted as a faithful brother.

Joseph's dreams (verses 5–11)

God gave Joseph an early glimpse of his future promotion, to support and comfort him through the long and painful troubles that lay ahead.

Joseph dreamed of advancement, but not of imprisonment.

Many young people beginning life are much the same: they imagine only success and pleasure, never the suffering they may encounter.

Joseph's brothers understood the dreams correctly, but hated their meaning. They committed crimes to prevent the prediction from coming true, yet became the very instruments of its fulfillment.

Something similar happened with Christ. The Jews understood what he said about his kingdom. Determined that he should not reign over them, they plotted his death. By crucifying him, they opened the way to the very exaltation they wanted to prevent.

Joseph obeys his father; his brothers plot to kill him (verses 12–22)

How readily Joseph obeyed his father's instructions! Children who receive particular affection from their parents should be particularly ready to obey them.

See how deliberately his brothers plotted against him. They intended to kill him with calculated malice, in cold blood.

“Everyone who hates his brother is a murderer” (1 John 3:15).

The sons of Jacob hated Joseph because their father loved him. New events, including his dreams, fed the resentment already festering in their hearts until they resolved to kill him.

God holds every heart in his hand. Reuben, the firstborn, had more reason than any of the others to be jealous of Joseph, yet he proved Joseph's best friend.

God overruled their actions to accomplish his own purpose: Joseph would save many people from death.

Joseph was also a picture of Christ, the beloved Son of his Father, hated by a wicked world. The Father sent him from his presence to visit us in great humility and love.

Christ came from heaven to earth to seek and save us. People plotted maliciously against him; his own people did not receive him, but crucified him.

He submitted to it willingly as part of his purpose to redeem and save us.

Joseph is sold (verses 23–30)

Joseph's brothers threw him into a pit to die of hunger and cold. How cruel were the supposed mercies of those who should have loved him!

They dismissed his distress and were not grieved by Joseph's suffering (Amos 6:6). While he languished in the pit, they sat down to eat.

They felt no remorse. Yet human wrath will praise God, and he will restrain whatever remains of it (Psalm 76:10).

Remarkably, the brothers were restrained from murdering Joseph. Just as remarkably, their decision to sell him was turned toward God's praise.

Jacob is deceived; Joseph is sold to Potiphar (verses 31–36)

Once Satan has taught people to commit one sin, he teaches them to hide it with another: theft and murder are covered with lies and false oaths.

But whoever conceals sin will not prosper for long. Joseph's brothers kept their dreadful secret for a time, but their wickedness eventually came to light and has now been made known to the world.

They sent their father Joseph's richly colored coat to cause him grief. Seeing it covered in blood, Jacob quickly assumed that a wild animal had torn Joseph apart.

Anyone who knows a parent's heart can imagine his agony.

His sons pretended to comfort him. What miserable, hypocritical comforters! If they had truly wanted to help, they could have told him the truth at once.

Sin has a strange power to harden the heart. Jacob refused to be comforted.

The more strongly we attach ourselves to any created thing, the more deeply we may suffer if it is taken away or becomes bitter to us. Excessive love often leads to excessive sorrow.

Wise parents do not raise their children in excessive luxury and ease. They cannot know what hardships their children may face before death.

The whole chapter leaves us marveling at God's providence.

The malicious brothers seem to have achieved their purpose. The merchants, interested only in profit and indifferent to what they trade, seem to have achieved theirs. Potiphar has acquired a fine young slave and has also obtained what he wanted.

Yet through all of this, God's plan is moving forward. Joseph's sale leads to Israel's descent into Egypt, then to Israel's deliverance through Moses, then to the establishment of true religion in the world, and ultimately to its spread among all nations through the gospel.

Thus human wrath will praise the Lord, and he will restrain the remainder.

Verses 1-4
In Joseph's history we see something of Christ, who was first humbled and then exalted. It also shows the lot of Christians, who must through many tribulations enter into the kingdom. It is a history that has none like it, for displaying the various workings of the human mind, both good and bad, and the singular providence of God in making use of them for fulfilling his purposes. Though Joseph was his father's darling, yet he was not bred up in idleness. Those do not truly love their children, who do not use them to business, and labour, and hardships. The fondling of children is with good reason called the spoiling of them. Those who are trained up to do nothing, are likely to be good for nothing. But Jacob made known his love, by dressing Joseph finer than the rest of his children. It is wrong for parents to make a difference between one child and another, unless there is great cause for it, by the children's dutifulness, or undutifulness. When parents make a difference, children soon notice it, and it leads to quarrels in families. Jacob's sons did that, when they were from under his eye, which they durst not have done at home with him; but Joseph gave his father an account of their ill conduct, that he might restrain them. Not as a tale-bearer, to sow discord, but as a faithful brother.
[Gen.37.5-Gen.37.11]
Verses 5-11
God gave Joseph betimes the prospect of his advancement, to support and comfort him under his long and grievous troubles. Observe, Joseph dreamed of his preferment, but he did not dream of his imprisonment. Thus many young people, when setting out in the world, think of nothing but prosperity and pleasure, and never dream of trouble. His brethren rightly interpreted the dream, though they abhorred the interpretation of it. While they committed crimes in order to defeat it, they were themselves the instruments of accomplishing it. Thus the Jews understood what Christ said of his kingdom. Determined that he should not reign over them, they consulted to put him to death; and by his crucifixion, made way for the exaltation they designed to prevent.
[Gen.37.12-Gen.37.22]
Verses 12-22
How readily does Joseph wait his father's orders! Those children who are best beloved by their parents, should be the most ready to obey them. See how deliberate Joseph's brethren were against him. They thought to slay him from malice aforethought, and in cold blood. Whosoever hateth his brother is a murderer, [1John.3.15] 1Jo 3:15. The sons of Jacob hated their brother because their father loved him. New occasions, as his dreams and the like, drew them on further; but this laid rankling in their hearts, till they resolved on his death. God has all hearts in his hands. Reuben had most reason to be jealous of Joseph, for he was the first-born; yet he proves his best friend. God overruled all to serve his own purpose, of making Joseph an instrument to save much people alive. Joseph was a type of Christ; for though he was the beloved Son of his Father, and hated by a wicked world, yet the Father sent him out of his bosom to visit us in great humility and love. He came from heaven to earth to seek and save us; yet then malicious plots were laid against him. His own not only received him not, but crucified him. This he submitted to, as a part of his design to redeem and save us.
[Gen.37.23-Gen.37.30]
Verses 23-30
They threw Joseph into a pit, to perish there with hunger and cold; so cruel were their tender mercies. They slighted him when he was in distress, and were not grieved for the affliction of Joseph, see [Amos.6.6] Am 6:6; for when he was pining in the pit, they sat down to eat bread. They felt no remorse of conscience for the sin. But the wrath of man shall praise God, and the remainder of wrath he will restrain, [Ps.76.10] Psa 76:10. Joseph's brethren were wonderfully restrained from murdering him, and their selling him as wonderfully turned to God's praise.
[Gen.37.31-Gen.37.36]
Verses 31-36
When Satan has taught men to commit one sin, he teaches them to try to conceal it with another; to hide theft and murder, with lying and false oaths: but he that covers his sin shall not prosper long. Joseph's brethren kept their own and one another's counsel for some time; but their villany came to light at last, and it is here published to the world. To grieve their father, they sent him Joseph's coat of colours; and he hastily thought, on seeing the bloody coat, that Joseph was rent in pieces. Let those that know the heart of a parent, suppose the agony of poor Jacob. His sons basely pretended to comfort him, but miserable, hypocritical comforters were they all. Had they really desired to comfort him, they might at once have done it, by telling the truth. The heart is strangely hardened by the deceitfulness of sin. Jacob refused to be comforted. Great affection to any creature prepares for so much the greater affliction, when it is taken from us, or made bitter to us: undue love commonly ends in undue grief. It is the wisdom of parents not to bring up children delicately, they know not to what hardships they may be brought before they die. From the whole of this chapter we see with wonder the ways of Providence. The malignant brothers seem to have gotten their ends; the merchants, who care not what they deal in so that they gain, have also obtained theirs; and Potiphar, having got a fine young slave, has obtained his! But God's designs are, by these means, in train for execution. This event shall end in Israel's going down to Egypt; that ends in their deliverance by Moses; that in setting up the true religion in the world; and that in the spread of it among all nations by the gospel. Thus the wrath of man shall praise the Lord, and the remainder thereof will he restrain.

Judah and his family (whole-chapter exposition)

This chapter tells the story of Judah and his family. It is such a troubling account that we may wonder why our Lord should descend from Judah, of all Jacob's sons (Hebrews 7:14).

But God shows us that his choice rests on grace, not personal merit. Christ came into the world to save sinners, even the worst of them.

We also learn that Christ's worthiness comes from himself, not from the people among his ancestors.

How little reason the Jews, whose name came from Judah, had for the boasting described in John 8:41!

What fearful examples God gives, through his judgments, of his complete hatred of sin.

Let us seek his grace to avoid even the appearance of sin.

And let the humility of Jesus make him still dearer to us. When he came to put away sin by sacrificing himself, he submitted to being born from a family line that included people such as those described here.

God is with Joseph in Potiphar's house (verses 1–6)

Our enemies may take away our outward signs of honor, but they cannot take away wisdom or grace.

They can separate us from friends, family, and country, but they cannot take away the Lord's presence.

They can deprive us of earthly blessings, rob us of freedom, and lock us in prison, but they cannot shut us out from fellowship with God, from the throne of grace, or from the blessings of salvation.

Joseph was blessed—wonderfully blessed—even in the house where he served as a slave.

When God is present with us, he makes what we do prosper.

Godly people are a blessing wherever they live. Faithful servants can be a blessing even if their position is low and they are little respected.

Sometimes the prosperity of wicked people comes, in one way or another, for the sake of the godly among them.

Here a wicked household was blessed because one good servant lived in it.

Joseph resists temptation (verses 7–12)

Physical beauty, in men or women, often becomes a trap both to the person who possesses it and to others.

We should therefore never become proud of beauty, and we must always watch carefully against the temptations that come with it.

We greatly need to make a covenant with our eyes, so that what we look at does not corrupt our hearts.

When lust gains control, people sacrifice decency, reputation, and conscience.

Potiphar's wife showed that her heart was entirely set on doing evil.

Satan had failed to overcome Joseph through the world's troubles and disapproval. Through them all, Joseph held firmly to his principles.

So Satan attacked him with pleasures—a temptation that has ruined more people than suffering has.

But God's grace enabled Joseph to resist and overcome. His escape was as striking a demonstration of divine power as the rescue of the three young men from the fiery furnace.

This particular sin could easily have entangled him.

The woman tempting him was his master's wife. Her favor might help him advance, while refusing her could turn her into a dangerous enemy.

The place and the time suited the temptation. And she urged him constantly and repeatedly.

Yet the almighty grace of God enabled Joseph to withstand this assault.

He remembered what he owed both to God and to his master.

Honor, justice, and gratitude all require us not to betray those who trust us, even if the betrayal could remain hidden.

Above all, Joseph would not offend his God.

He considered three things.

First, who was being tempted? He was a man in covenant with God, someone who openly professed faith and belonged to him.

Second, what was he being tempted to do? Others might call the sin a small matter, but Joseph refused to think of it that way.

Call sin by its proper name; never make it seem less serious than it is. Sins of this kind are great wickedness, exceedingly sinful.

Third, against whom would the sin be committed? Against God—against his nature, his rule, his love, and his purposes.

Those who love God therefore hate sin.

By God's grace, Joseph overcame the temptation by getting away from it. He did not remain to negotiate with it; he fled as though escaping for his life.

If we truly intend not to do evil, we must flee like a bird escaping a trap or a deer escaping a hunter.

Joseph is falsely accused (verses 13–18)

Joseph's mistress failed to make him guilty, so she sought revenge instead.

Those who have broken the restraints of decency may also disregard the restraints of truth.

It is nothing new for the best of people to be falsely accused of the worst crimes by people who are themselves deeply guilty.

How good it is to know that a day of disclosure is coming, when everyone will appear as they truly are.

God is with Joseph in prison (verses 19–23)

Joseph's master believed the accusation.

Henry considers it likely that Potiphar chose this prison because it was the worst available. But God intended it as the path toward Joseph's future honor.

God acknowledged Joseph and vindicated him.

Far from friends and relatives, he had no one to help or comfort him. Yet the Lord was with him and showed him mercy.

A person who has a clear conscience in prison has a good God there as well.

God caused the keeper of the prison to look favorably on Joseph and entrust him with responsibility for its affairs.

A good person will do good wherever he is, becoming a blessing even in imprisonment or exile.

But as we look at Joseph, let us not forget Jesus.

He suffered temptation without sin. He was slandered, persecuted, and imprisoned without cause; yet through the cross he ascended to the throne.

May God enable us to follow him in submission and suffering, and finally to the same place of glory.

Beauty either in men or women, often proves a snare both to themselves and others. This forbids pride in it, and requires constant watchfulness against the temptation that attends it. We have great need to make a covenant with our eyes, lest the eyes infect the heart. When lust has got power, decency, and reputation, and conscience, are all sacrificed. Potiphar's wife showed that her heart was fully set to do evil. Satan, when he found he could not overcome Joseph with the troubles and the frowns of the world, for in them he still held fast his principle, assaulted him with pleasures, which have ruined more than the former. This sin was one which might most easily beset him. The tempter was his mistress, one whose favour would help him forward; and it was at his utmost peril if he slighted her, and made her his enemy. The time and place favoured the temptation. To all this was added frequent, constant urging. The almighty grace of God enabled Joseph to overcome this assault of the enemy. He urges what he owed both to God and his master. We are bound in honour, as well as justice and gratitude, not in any thing to wrong those who place trust in us, how secretly soever it may be done. He would not offend his God. Three arguments Joseph urges upon himself. 1. He considers who he was that was tempted. One in covenant with God, who professed religion and relation to him. 2. What the sin was to which he was tempted. Others might look upon it as a small matter; but Joseph did not so think of it. Call sin by its own name, and never lessen it. Let sins of this nature always be looked upon as great wickedness, as exceedingly sinful. 3. Against whom he was tempted to sin, against God. Sin is against God, against his nature and his dominion, against his love and his design. Those that love God, for this reason hate sin. The grace of God enabled Joseph to overcome the temptation, by avoiding the temper. He would not stay to parley with the temptation, but fled from it, as escaping for his life. Joseph's mistress, having tried in vain to make him a guilty man, endeavoured to be avenged on him. Those that have broken the bonds of modesty, will never be held by the bonds of truth. It is no new thing for the best of men to be falsely accused of the worst of crimes, by those who themselves are the worst of criminals. It is well there is a day of discovery coming, in which all shall appear in their true characters.

Verses 19-23
Joseph's master believed the accusation. Potiphar, it is likely, chose that prison, because it was the worst; but God designed to open the way to Joseph's honour. Joseph was owned and righted by his God. He was away from all his friends and relations; he had none to help or comfort him; but the Lord was with Joseph, and showed him mercy. Those that have a good conscience in a prison, have a good God there. God gave him favour in the sight of the keeper of the prison; he trusted him to manage the affairs of the prison. A good man will do good wherever he is, and will be a blessing even in bonds and banishment. Let us not forget, through Joseph, to look unto Jesus, who suffered being tempted, yet without sin; who was slandered, and persecuted, and imprisoned, but without cause; who by the cross ascended to the throne. May we be enabled to follow the same path in submitting and in suffering, to the same place of glory.

The cupbearer's and baker's dreams (verses 1–19)

The chief cupbearer and the chief baker were troubled less by their imprisonment than by their dreams.

God has more than one way of bringing sorrow to a person's spirit.

Those who are in distress often find relief simply in being noticed.

Is there a good reason for it? Is there no comfort sufficient to outweigh it, whatever the cause may be?

Ministers of God's word are likewise interpreters. They cannot change the message they have been given.

When they faithfully declare it, they are not to blame if people dislike what they hear.

Joseph did not bring up his brothers' cruelty in selling him. Nor did he dwell on the wrong done to him by his master's wife and his master.

He simply stated his own innocence.

When we must defend ourselves, we should avoid speaking badly of others as far as we can.

Let us be content to establish our innocence without reproaching others for their guilt.

The cupbearer forgets Joseph (verses 20–23)

Joseph's interpretation of both dreams came true on the exact day he had announced.

It was Pharaoh's birthday. His servants gathered before him, and the two prisoners' cases were considered.

We can all benefit from taking note of our own birthdays.

They give us an opportunity to thank God for the mercy of our birth, to grieve over the sins of our lives, and to look toward the day of our death as better than the day of our birth.

Yet it is strange that worldly people, so attached to life here, celebrate the passing of another year in their short time on earth.

Christians have reason to rejoice both that they were born and that they are drawing nearer to the end of sin and sorrow, and to everlasting happiness.

But the chief cupbearer did not remember Joseph. He forgot him, even though Joseph had done him good.

We should not be surprised if love is repaid with hatred or kindness with neglect.

How quickly people at ease forget those who are still suffering!

Through this disappointment, Joseph learned to trust in God alone.

We cannot expect too little from people or too much from God.

Let us not forget our Redeemer's sufferings, promises, and love.

We blame the cupbearer for his ingratitude toward Joseph, but we are far more ungrateful toward the Lord Jesus.

Joseph only foretold the cupbearer's release. Christ actually accomplished ours, pleading for us before the King of kings.

Yet we forget him, despite frequent reminders and despite our own promises never to do so.

How poorly we repay him—like a foolish, unwise people.
classic_reading:
[Gen.40.1-Gen.40.19]
Chapter 40
Chapter Outline
The chief butler and baker of Pharaoh in prison, Their dreams interpreted by Joseph. | (1-19) |
The ingratitude of the chief butler. | (20-23) |
Verses 1-19
It was not so much the prison that made the butler and baker sad, as their dreams. God has more ways than one to sadden the spirits. Joseph had compassion towards them. Let us be concerned for the sadness of our brethren's countenances. It is often a relief to those that are in trouble to be noticed. Also learn to look into the causes of our own sorrow. Is there a good reason? Is there not comfort sufficient to balance it, whatever it is? Why art thou cast down, O my soul? Joseph was careful to ascribe the glory to God. The chief butler's dream foretold his advancement. The chief baker's dream his death. It was not Joseph's fault that he brought the baker no better tidings. And thus ministers are but interpreters; they cannot make the thing otherwise than it is: if they deal faithfully, and their message prove unpleasing, it is not their fault. Joseph does not reflect upon his brethren that sold him; nor does he reflect on the wrong done him by his mistress and his master, but mildly states his own innocence. When we are called on to clear ourselves, we should carefully avoid, as much as may be, speaking ill of others. Let us be content to prove ourselves innocent, and not upbraid others with their guilt.
[Gen.40.20-Gen.40.23]
Verses 20-23
Joseph's interpretation of the dreams came to pass on the very day fixed. On Pharaoh's birth-day, all his servants attended him, and then the cases of these two came to be looked into. We may all profitably take notice of our birth-days, with thankfulness for the mercies of our birth, sorrow for the sinfulness of our lives, and expectation of the day of our death, as better than the day of our birth. But it seems strange that worldly people, who are so fond of living here, should rejoice at the end of one year after another of their short span of life. A Christian has cause to rejoice that he was born, also that he comes nearer to the end of his sin and sorrow, and nearer to his everlasting happiness. The chief butler remembered not Joseph, but forgot him. Joseph had deserved well at his hands, yet he forgot him. We must not think it strange, if in this world we have hatred shown us for our love, and slights for our kindness. See how apt those who are themselves at ease are to forget others in distress. Joseph learned by his disappointment to trust in God only. We cannot expect too little from man, nor too much from God. Let us not forget the sufferings, promises, and love of our Redeemer. We blame the chief butler's ingratitude to Joseph, yet we ourselves act much more ungratefully to the Lord Jesus. Joseph had but foretold the chief butler's enlargement, but Christ wrought out ours; he mediated with the King of Kings for us; yet we forget him, though often reminded of him, and though we have promised never to forget him. Thus ill do we requite Him, like foolish people and unwise.
